cues.text: A Young Mother's Choice
In the year 203, in the North African city of Carthage , a decree of the Emperor Septimius Severus forbade conversion to Christianity under pain of death.

Among those swept up were several catechumens preparing for baptism: Vibia Perpetua , a well-born young woman of about twenty-two, still nursing her infant son, and Felicitas , a slave girl who was eight months pregnant.
Perpetua's own father, a pagan, came to her in prison again and again, begging her, for the sake of her family and her child, to renounce the name she had taken.

She tells us, in words that still move us today, that she answered him simply by pointing to a water jar and asking whether it could be called by any other name than what it was — and so, she said, neither could she be called anything other than what she was: a Christian.
A Diary Written in Prison
What makes Perpetua's witness so extraordinary is that we possess her own words, set down in the darkness of her cell — the earliest substantial writing by a Christian woman to come down to us.

In it she records her fears, her visions, and above all her unwavering resolve, describing a dream in which she climbed a great bronze ladder studded with dangerous weapons to reach a garden where an old shepherd fed her cheese from his flock, a vision she understood as God's promise of what awaited her beyond her trial.
Across the gulf of eighteen centuries, we can still hear, in these pages, the voice of a mother, a daughter, and a believer — utterly human, utterly afraid, and utterly resolved, all at once.
Felicity's Answer to the Guards
Felicity, meanwhile, feared that her pregnancy might delay her martyrdom and separate her from her companions, for Roman law forbade the execution of a pregnant woman.

Two days before the appointed date, in the pain of premature labor, she cried out, and when a guard mocked her, asking how she would endure the beasts if she could not bear this, she answered him with words the Church has never forgotten: that now she suffered what she herself was suffering, but in the arena, another would be in her, suffering for her, because she would be suffering for him.
She gave birth to a healthy daughter, entrusted at once to the care of a Christian sister, and went to her death alongside Perpetua only two days later.
Two Women, One Faith
On the day of the games, Perpetua and Felicity, along with their companions Revocatus, Saturninus, and Saturus, were led into the amphitheater of Carthage.

The two women, still weak from Felicity's recent delivery, were exposed together to a wild heifer chosen, in a cruelty typical of the age, precisely because it matched their sex; battered and torn, they helped each other to their feet, and Perpetua, we are told, straightened her disheveled hair, unwilling to appear as one in mourning at what she considered her hour of glory.
When the beasts had not finished the work, the martyrs were finally dispatched by the sword.

Perpetua's own executioner, a young and inexperienced gladiator, faltered and struck a glancing blow; it was Perpetua herself who is said to have guided his shaking hand to her throat, unwilling that so great a gift as her own life should be anything less than freely and completely given.
Legacy
The account of their Passion, drawn largely from Perpetua's own diary and completed by an eyewitness, was so treasured by the early African Church that St.
Augustine himself, two centuries later, had to remind his own congregation not to place it above the canonical Scriptures, so widely was it read at the liturgy.
Their names endure today in the very heart of the Mass, spoken aloud in the Roman Canon among the great martyrs of the early Church.

Across every century since, Perpetua and Felicity have stood as an image of the dignity Christ confers on every human life without exception — noblewoman and slave, mother and daughter, made one in a friendship that death itself could not sever, and that continues to summon believers today to the same total, free gift of self.
